mediaItem.keyStats:
- Chicago ranked first in the number of exonerations in the US for the sixth year in a row.
- Chicago has paid over $735 million in connection with wrongful conviction lawsuits.
- Over 200 wrongful conviction cases currently pending in the Northern District of Illinois.
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction tells the harrowing story of Roosevelt Miles, wrongfully convicted in Chicago for a murder he did not commit.  Miles details his challenging childhood and early brushes with the law before being ensnared by corrupt Area 5 gang unit detectives, including the notorious Anthony Wojczyk.  Coerced witness testimony and fabricated evidence led to his 1996 conviction and a 60-year sentence, despite his innocence.  The podcast highlights the systemic issues within the Chicago justice system, including police misconduct and ineffective legal representation. After serving 28 years and persistent legal battles aided by the Bond Jean Law Group, Miles was finally exonerated in 2024.  The episode underscores the immense personal toll of wrongful convictions and the ongoing fight for justice and systemic reform in Chicago.

contributingFactorsRaw: Eyewitness misidentification (Octavius Morris coerced to identify him)
Police misconduct (Anthony Wojczyk coerced witnesses, beat Roosevelt Miles, fabricated evidence)
Ineffective assistance of counsel (Trial defender failed to call alibi witness and properly investigate third-party suspect)
organizationsInvolvedRaw: Bond Jean Law Group (represented Roosevelt in post-conviction)
Exoneration Project in Chicago (mentioned in context of Wojczyk pattern evidence)
innocenceLawyersRaw: Ashley Cohn from the Bond Jean Law Group is interviewed in the podcast episode and is highlighted as being instrumental in his exoneration, alongside Jennifer Bongine. They are described as "young ladies [who] brought me out of hell" and "earth angels."
featuredIndividual.crossReference: Not explicitly stated if in exoneree database, but highly likely given exoneration and public case.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: Shaharan Brandon was shot dead during a robbery in Chicago in November 1992. His girlfriend, Octavius Morris, initially stated she didn't see the shooter's face and described teenage shooters. Another witness, Sandra Birch, also gave a similar initial description.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Recanted eyewitness identification from Octavius Morris, who under oath claimed Roosevelt Miles was the shooter (after initially saying it wasn't him).
Circumstantial and "garbled" testimony from Deborah Lenore, suggesting Roosevelt was near the scene after the shooting.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes:
- Public defender failed to call alibi witness (Michael Hooker).
- Public defender did not adequately explore the possibility of a third-party offender (Octavius Morris's former boyfriend).
- Public defender's representation was described by Roosevelt as ineffective, stating "he barely ejected a lot of these what was brought out."
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Recantation affidavit from Octavius Morris detailing police coercion by Detective Anthony Wojczyk.
Affidavit from alibi witness Michael Hooker, confirming Roosevelt's location at the time of the shooting.
Evidence of Anthony Wojczyk's pattern and practice of misconduct, including coercing confessions and manipulating witnesses in other cases.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Not detailed in the transcript. The focus is on Roosevelt Miles' wrongful conviction and the flaws in the investigation, not on identifying the actual perpetrator.  Octavius Morris's former boyfriend was mentioned as a potential lead that was not properly investigated.

keyQuotesRaw: Roosevelt Miles: "You can kill me because I'm not going to say that that I didn't do." (Regarding police coercion)
Roosevelt Miles: "I knew I knew I knew I'm going to prison." (During the trial when realizing the jury was swayed)
Ashley Cohn: "Chicago ranked the first in the number of exonerations across the United States. They are the wrongful conviction capital of the world."
Roosevelt Miles: "I'm not bitter. I just hate that I lost my parents seven months apart and 16 and 17." (Reflecting on the personal impact)
Roosevelt Miles: "I just like to see Wojie have his day in court where everybody sees his true colors and who this man really is." (Desire for accountability)
systemicIssuesRaw: Police misconduct and corruption within the Chicago Police Department, specifically Area 5 gang unit and Detective Anthony Wojczyk.
Coercion of witnesses and fabrication of evidence by police.
Lengthy and arduous post-conviction process, taking decades for exoneration.
Difficulties in proving "actual innocence" for compensation in Illinois.
Resistance from the State's Attorney's office to fully acknowledge and rectify past misconduct, even in the face of overwhelming evidence.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Reforming the justice system in Illinois, particularly in Chicago, to prevent wrongful convictions.
Increased accountability for police misconduct and corruption.
Early review and settlement of wrongful conviction cases by the city of Chicago to avoid lengthy litigation and further harm to exonerees.
Legislative changes to facilitate compensation for exonerees and streamline the process for proving actual innocence.
Audience call to action to support Roosevelt Miles' nonprofit "help break the chain" and to be aware of wrongful conviction issues.
personalNarrativeRaw: Roosevelt Miles endured 28 years of wrongful imprisonment, losing precious time with family, including his parents who passed away while he was incarcerated.
He experienced trauma and violence in prison.
Despite the immense injustice, Roosevelt expresses resilience, forgiveness, and a desire to help others through his nonprofit.
He highlights the crucial role of his legal team, Ashley Cohn and Jennifer Bongine, in securing his freedom and giving him back his life.
